extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans, and researchers interested in John Green and contemporary young-adult literature
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive Wikipedia biography of author John Green covering his life, works, adaptations, public activities, reception, controversies, and awards. Contains descriptive and critical commentary about his books and influence on YA literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: GreenLit characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Books described as 'GreenLit' contain 'sharp dialogue, defective authority figures, occasional boozing, unrequited crushes, and one or more heartbreaking twists.' (A. J. Jacobs' description cited in The New York Times review cited on the page.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a shorthand to describe a set of recurring stylistic/content elements in contemporary YA fiction associated with John Green; implies that evaluating a work in this sub-genre can consider presence and execution of those elements (dialogue quality, portrayal of authority figures, tone, romantic dynamics, and impactful emotional moments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic, genuine, relatable characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for Green's work highlights 'authentic, genuine, relatable characters' as a distinguishing quality (quote attributed to Zareen Jaffery, executive editor at Simon & Schuster Books for Young Readers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of YA fiction often consider whether characters feel realistic and relatable to readers; this criterion is tied to commercial and critical reception and to the so-called 'John Green effect' on the market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional truthfulness and maturity
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics praised works like Turtles All the Way Down as 'truthful and authentic' and The Anthropocene Reviewed (nonfiction) as 'most mature, compelling, and beautifully written yet,' indicating a critical standard of emotional honesty and literary maturity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should consider whether prose and narrative voice convey emotional truth, avoid cliché in a way that still resonates, and demonstrate growth/maturity appropriate to the genre or shift between fiction and nonfiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deconstruction of tropes (e.g., 'Manic Pixie Dream Girl')
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of criticism that Green writes 'Manic Pixie Dream Girls' is countered by claims (and authorial intent) that works such as Paper Towns serve as a deconstruction of that trope; Green states the novels aim to show such characters are 'not a miracle... [they] were a girl.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating characterization, consider whether the work interrogates, subverts, or merely perpetuates problematic tropes; credible deconstruction should make clear the trope's limitations and portray characters as full persons rather than plot devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of dehumanizing or derogatory language
rubrics_metrics.description: John Green publicly apologized for using the word 'retarded' in Paper Towns, stating regret and recognizing that dehumanizing language undermines a book's intent to humanize others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and evaluators should avoid or critique language that dehumanizes groups or individuals; sensitivity to slurs and dated/derogatory terms is a criterion for contemporary literary assessment and for ethical considerations in publication and classroom/library contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content likely to prompt challenges or bans (offensive language / sexual content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several of Green's books have faced banning attempts; Looking for Alaska was the most challenged book of 2015 with complaints about 'offensive language' and 'sexually explicit descriptions.' The page documents instances where The Fault in Our Stars was removed/moved in library collections due to policies targeting language about sexuality, reproduction, profanity, and criminal acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical/content evaluation of YA works should note that explicit sexual content, profanity, or other material deemed 'offensive' by some communities may prompt challenges in school/library settings; this is a procedural/administrative consequence that can inform decisions about target audience, labeling, and use in educational contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial and critical impact metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures cited on the page include New York Times Best Seller list placement, translations into 55 languages, more than 50 million copies in print worldwide, numerous awards and honors (Printz Award, Edgar Allan Poe Award, bestseller statuses), and sustained presence on bestseller lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impact and success can be evaluated by bestseller status, sales/circulation numbers, translations, and awards; these are objective/cumulative metrics that indicate cultural reach and reception but do not by themselves measure literary quality.
